title: The Gang Chokes

jokes.text: Mac interrupts a heartfelt toast to ask why there's no blue food on the menu
jokes.setup: Someone is trying to give a sincere toast/speech at a fancy restaurant
jokes.punchline: Mac derails it immediately by fixating on whether there is blue food on the menu
jokes.explanation: Classic Mac obliviousness — derailing a sincere moment for something absurd. The 'blue food' fixation pays off across the episode, so this is both funny on its own and sets up future jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I don't see any blue on this menu.

jokes.text: Oh, God. You people. / Ugh, this guy again. / Come on, man. What are you doing here? This isn't Guigino's. / Yeah, I thought you moved.
jokes.setup: A waiter approaches the table in a fancy restaurant to take orders.
jokes.punchline: The entire gang immediately treats the new waiter as a recurring annoyance, as though they know him personally, and are upset he is there — implying they drive service staff away everywhere they go.
jokes.explanation: The gang's collective awfulness toward service staff is a classic Sunny bit. The added layer — that they think they know him, that they can't get away from him — suggests they are so terrible that waiters haunt them or that they've alienated all the staff everywhere. Solid ensemble gag.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: The best foods are blue.

jokes.text: Charlie defends blue food: 'The best foods are blue.'
jokes.setup: Mac asks why you'd want to eat blue food
jokes.punchline: Charlie responds with total conviction: 'The best foods are blue.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie logic — absolute confidence in a completely nonsensical statement. The economy is excellent (five words, total conviction) and it's completely character-specific. Only Charlie Kelly would say this and believe it.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Now, Dennis, what will I be having this evening?

jokes.text: The waiter they all hate appears: 'What's in them little bowls? Blue, I hope.'
jokes.setup: An apparently despised waiter reappears unexpectedly; the gang can't escape him
jokes.punchline: His first question after a dramatic reappearance is whether the amuse-bouche is blue
jokes.explanation: The gag of the inescapable waiter layered with the blue food running gag is a smart double-stacking. His reappearance is well-timed and his callback to 'blue' ties the threads together economically.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, God. You people.

jokes.text: Frank: 'We don't want compliments, we want food. If I wanted a compliment, I'd walk into a bar.'
jokes.setup: Waiter explains the amuse-bouche is 'compliments from the chef'
jokes.punchline: Frank takes 'compliments' literally and says he can get those at a bar, implying he receives flattery from strangers — a deeply delusional self-image
jokes.explanation: Sharp wordplay (literal vs. figurative 'compliments') married to Frank's oblivious self-aggrandizement. Economical and quotable. The implication that Frank regularly gets compliments at bars is funnier than the wordplay alone.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Ugh, this guy again.

jokes.text: Dennis offers to throw water in Dee's face; Dee asks 'do you want me to throw my glass of water in her face?' Dennis: 'Well, don't ask. Just do.'
jokes.setup: Dee says something that annoys the group at the dinner table
jokes.punchline: Dennis's casual cruelty toward his sister — treating violence against her as a reasonable restaurant activity — and his irritation that Mac asked permission first
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis Reynolds contempt for Dee, amplified by Mac's pathetic need to seek Dennis's approval even for acts of petty violence. The 'don't ask, just do' punchline is sharp and characteristically Dennis.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: We can't get away from you.

jokes.text: Charlie offers to pre-chew Frank's amuse-bouche for him: 'You haven't had your teeth sharpened in a bit. I better chew it.'
jokes.setup: Charlie notices Frank isn't chewing well
jokes.punchline: Charlie casually offers to chew Frank's food for him — and mentions Frank gets his teeth 'sharpened,' presented as a normal grooming activity
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character-specific comedy. Only Charlie and Frank's deeply weird codependent relationship would produce casual food-chewing as an act of care. 'Teeth sharpening' as routine maintenance is a perfect absurdist detail delivered deadpan. The other character's confused 'He gets his teeth sharpened?' reaction amplifies it. This is what distinguishes Sunny from lesser shows — the joke is entirely rooted in who these people are.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: If I wanted a compliment, I'd walk into a bar.

jokes.text: Frank begins choking while the gang watches for an extended beat and does nothing
jokes.setup: Frank starts choking on his food at the restaurant
jokes.punchline: The gang watches him choke with apparent inaction — the dark premise that these terrible people won't help their friend/family member
jokes.explanation: The central premise of the episode and the show's thesis statement in one moment: these people are so awful they won't perform the most basic act of human decency. The timestamps (01:15 choking, 01:35 'Hmm.', 01:40 waiter giving specials, 01:44 'Oh my God!') suggest a devastating long pause where the gang just watches. This is structurally excellent dark comedy — the horror is in the gap.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You don't chew no good anymore. You want me to chew that up for you?

jokes.text: Beat: 'Hmm.' — a character (likely Dennis) contemplates whether to save Frank
jokes.setup: Frank is actively choking; a moment passes
jokes.punchline: The only response is a contemplative 'Hmm.' — as if saving a choking man requires real deliberation
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode precisely because it's one word — or barely even that. 'Hmm.' as a response to a man choking to death is devastating in its economy. The entirety of Dennis's sociopathy is contained in that syllable. Perfect example of Sunny's restraint when it counts.

dialogue.line: He gets his teeth sharpened?

jokes.text: Waiter arrives to describe specials while Frank is mid-choke
jokes.setup: Frank has been choking; chaos is presumably visible
jokes.punchline: The waiter blithely begins describing specials anyway — either oblivious or choosing to ignore the medical emergency
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of restaurant normalcy against an ongoing medical emergency is excellent comedic timing. Extends and deepens the choking joke by adding a third party's indifference.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I think he's choking.

jokes.text: Dennis's excuse for not saving Frank: 'Maybe I thought that's how you wanted to go out, Frank.'
jokes.setup: Frank is furious that Dennis didn't save him from choking
jokes.punchline: Dennis claims he may have been respecting Frank's choice of death — an absurd rationalization that reveals he genuinely considered letting him die
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis sociopathy delivered as reasonable logic. Only Dennis Reynolds would frame not saving a choking man as being thoughtful about his death preferences. Character-specific and darkly funny.

jokes.text: Frank lists his unwanted death scenarios: 'in a hospital bed or getting spit-roasted by two Latin King gang members in prison'
jokes.setup: Dennis claims he doesn't know how Frank wants to die
jokes.punchline: Frank responds that he's been very clear about how he DOESN'T want to die — the second option (prison gang rape) is delivered with complete equivalence to the first
jokes.explanation: Exceptional. The structure is perfect: 'hospital bed' is the expected answer, 'spit-roasted by two Latin King gang members in prison' is the deranged escalation. Frank's history (the specificity of Latin Kings, the specificity of prison, the specificity of two) implies this fear is rooted in something real, which makes it funnier. This is a quotable, Sunny-defining line.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You only ever talk about how you don't want to die, like in a hospital bed or getting spit-roasted by two Latin King gang members in prison.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Who are watching me choke to death with pleasure in their eyes.'
jokes.setup: Dennis says Frank was surrounded by his friends
jokes.punchline: Frank clarifies: surrounded by friends who had pleasure in their eyes while watching him die
jokes.explanation: Good economical comeback that also advances the dark truth — these people really might have enjoyed watching Frank choke. 'Pleasure in their eyes' is a vivid and quotable phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You mash it too thin. You take all the flavor out of it. You get all the nutrients. I get all the mush.

jokes.text: Dennis admits he was 'a little mad' at Frank for not letting him finish his speech about blue food on the menu
jokes.setup: Dennis was asked why he didn't save Frank
jokes.punchline: His reason for possibly letting Frank die was petty annoyance at being interrupted during a toast — specifically about blue food
jokes.explanation: The callback to the blue food moment as the stated reason Dennis nearly let Frank die is a satisfying structural payoff. Dennis's pettiness elevated to potentially lethal levels is classic character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I used to do cool shit, Frank! I used to be cool!

jokes.text: Frank tells Charlie he won't chew his food anymore: 'You mash it too thin. You take all the flavor out of it. You get all the nutrients. I get all the mush.'
jokes.setup: Frank is threatening to leave Charlie
jokes.punchline: Frank's specific complaint about Charlie's food-chewing — that Charlie keeps all the nutrients and flavor for himself and gives Frank only mush — is delivered as a legitimate grievance in a co-dependent relationship
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best jokes in the episode. The specificity of the complaint — not just 'I don't like it' but a detailed nutritional breakdown of who gets what from the chewing arrangement — is brilliantly absurd. 'You get all the nutrients, I get all the mush' has perfect internal rhythm and logic. Only Frank and Charlie could have this argument. The concept of a food-chewing relationship with specific nutritional inequities is wholly original.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: getting spit-roasted by two Latin King gang members in prison

jokes.text: Charlie: 'Do you think I WANT to chew your food?'
jokes.setup: Frank complains about Charlie's food-chewing quality
jokes.punchline: Charlie implies that pre-chewing Frank's food is an act of selfless sacrifice that Frank is not appreciating — suggesting Charlie hates doing it but does it anyway, which is somehow worse
jokes.explanation: The implication that Charlie performs this disgusting act as an obligation — not out of joy — adds a layer of tragic codependency to the absurdity. Excellent character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Why do I still have to order your dinners for you? And why is it up to me to decide whether or not you're going to save a man's life?

jokes.text: Charlie declares he 'used to do cool shit' before chewing Frank's food consumed his identity: 'I used to be cool!'
jokes.setup: Charlie is breaking up with Frank over food-chewing duties
jokes.punchline: Charlie insists he was 'young and cool' before Frank's food-chewing took that from him — which is obviously never true of Charlie Kelly
jokes.explanation: The gap between Charlie's self-image ('young and cool') and the reality of who Charlie Kelly is provides strong ironic comedy. Frank's flat 'I'm cool.' in response is a perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: If you told me to.

jokes.text: Frank's response to Charlie's speech: 'I'm cool.'
jokes.setup: Charlie delivers an impassioned speech about how he used to be cool before Frank
jokes.punchline: Frank's only response is a flat, unaffected 'I'm cool.' — either not understanding the point or simply not caring
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Charlie speech. Two words, maximum impact. Frank completely ignoring Charlie's emotional crisis to assert his own coolness is classic Frank Reynolds. The economy is flawless.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Pizza man, pizza man, I got pizza here, who wants pizza man?

jokes.text: Mac: 'I would've stepped in, but, of course, I was taking my cues from you.' Dennis: 'Why?'
jokes.setup: Post-choking debrief; Mac explains why he didn't save Frank
jokes.punchline: Mac's excuse for not saving a choking man is that Dennis hadn't told him to — revealing Mac's total dependency and Dennis's irritated 'Why?' punctures the absurdity
jokes.explanation: The Mac-Dennis codependency expressed in its darkest form: Mac won't save a dying man without instructions. Dennis's frustrated 'Why?' is perfect — he finds this pathetic even as the show (and we) find it hilarious. Excellent character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What are you, like, in your 40s?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: As are you.

jokes.text: After midnight? What are you, like, in your 40s? / Yeah. As are you. / Yeah.
jokes.setup: Dennis complains it's after midnight for Charlie showing up.
jokes.punchline: Charlie mocks Dennis for caring about bedtime as something only 40-year-olds worry about. Dennis confirms they are both in their 40s. Charlie just says 'yeah.' The self-awareness deflates both of them.
jokes.explanation: Sharp, self-aware exchange. The show rarely acknowledges the characters' ages, so when Charlie's insult immediately collapses on itself — Dennis confirming they're both 40s, Charlie's flat 'yeah' — it's both funny and oddly poignant. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I actually ate all the cheese on the walk over, so... no cheese!

jokes.text: Mac: 'I-I would've saved you, Dennis. I would have saved you. If you told me to.'
jokes.setup: Dennis laments that no one would save him if he were choking
jokes.punchline: Mac reassures Dennis he would save him — but only if told to — the conditional completely undermining the reassurance
jokes.explanation: The 'if you told me to' caveat is the perfect punchline — it arrives just as the audience relaxes into what seemed like genuine reassurance. Mac's obliviousness to how this sounds is entirely in character. Highly quotable within the episode's context.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Don't worry about that, though. It's all good. I ate the crust, too.

jokes.text: Mac arrives after midnight with a pizza box that he has eaten entirely — crust, cheese, sauce — separately, leaving only an empty box
jokes.setup: Mac arrives supposedly with pizza as a peace offering
jokes.punchline: He ate all components separately on the walk over — the cheese, then the crust, then slurped the sauce — and arrived with an empty box
jokes.explanation: Genuinely original escalating absurdity — the joke gets funnier with each component Mac reveals he ate. The best part is 'you ate them all separately... and then came over with an empty pizza box?' — the structural reveal is impeccably timed. Dennis's summary is a perfect button: 'So you came over with a box of tomato sauce?' → 'Actually I slurped that up too.' This is excellent Sunny-caliber escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Actually, I slurped that up, too, because that was just kind of looking good

jokes.text: Dennis: 'So you came over with a box of tomato sauce?' / Mac: 'Actually, I slurped that up, too.'
jokes.setup: Dennis thinks Mac at least brought tomato sauce
jokes.punchline: Mac also consumed the sauce on the walk over, completing his total destruction of the pizza before arrival
jokes.explanation: The final beat of the pizza escalation — after the cheese and crust reveals, the sauce reveal is the unexpected third stab that makes the joke land fully. 'I slurped that up, too, because that was just kind of looking good' — the casual self-justification is perfect. The structure of the three-part reveal is classically excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: So you ate them all separately... all the elements... and then came over with an empty pizza box?

jokes.text: Dennis: 'It's the suggestion of food.'
jokes.setup: Mac arrives with an empty pizza box after midnight as a gesture
jokes.punchline: Dennis characterizes Mac's empty box as 'the suggestion of food' — precise, withering, and somehow correct
jokes.explanation: Four words, perfectly chosen. 'The suggestion of food' is both precise comedy writing and a genuinely original formulation. It's the kind of line that people quote. Dennis at his most withering and articulate.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I got a pretty good rush from a man almost dying right in front of me. I-I liked it

jokes.text: Dee barges in after midnight to describe nearly being hit by an Uber and the 'rush' she got from Frank almost dying
jokes.setup: Late-night apartment scene; Dennis and Mac are having a tense conversation
jokes.punchline: Dee crashes in, excited that she got a 'pretty good rush' from watching Frank almost die, and then nearly got hit by an Uber while spacing out about it
jokes.explanation: Establishes Dee's season arc (thrill-seeking) but the joke itself is a bit labored. 'Long story short' and the extended setup dilute the punch. The 'rush' revelation is good but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You're so good at telling stories. So concise.

jokes.text: Dennis cannot eat cheese (poison), crust (gluten), or sauce (sugar) — Charlie progressively eliminates every part of the pizza
jokes.setup: Charlie brings pizza as a peace offering; Dennis has dietary restrictions
jokes.punchline: Each element of pizza is eliminated one by one for a different health reason, leaving nothing
jokes.explanation: Good escalation structure — each element's removal sets up the next. Dennis's health obsession is a known character trait weaponized here for a bit with a clean trajectory toward the absurd conclusion.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I wish it did hit you.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'You're so good at telling stories. So concise.' / 'I wish it did hit you.'
jokes.setup: Dee finishes her rambling near-death story
jokes.punchline: Dennis's sarcastic 'so concise' about her terrible storytelling, then immediately wishing the Uber had actually hit her
jokes.explanation: Standard Dennis-on-Dee contempt. The 'concise' sarcasm is good; 'I wish it did hit you' is reliable but not exceptional. Competent sibling cruelty comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Go to bed? What are you, 40?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We're the same age!

jokes.text: Dennis's breakdown: 'It's the middle of the night. I'm surrounded by lunatics.' Dee: 'You're one of the lunatics!'
jokes.setup: Dennis declares he can't be around these people anymore
jokes.punchline: Dee correctly points out Dennis is himself one of the lunatics, which he completely ignores
jokes.explanation: A reliable Sunny move — Dennis declaring himself above the chaos he is entirely responsible for — but this is a fairly standard deployment of it.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Uh, Dennis, should I go to bed, too?' Dennis: 'I don't care!' Mac: 'He said yes, I think?'
jokes.setup: Dennis storms off to bed declaring independence from everyone
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately reverts to needing Dennis's permission to go to sleep — interpreting 'I don't care' as an affirmative answer
jokes.explanation: Perfect running gag payoff — Mac's dependency has escalated to needing permission to sleep. The 'He said yes, I think?' as Mac convinces himself that 'I don't care' means yes is a lovely character detail. Excellent integration of the episode's Mac-Dennis dependency theme.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm moving in.

jokes.text: Mac's logic: 'I should probably go to sleep because we depend on each other. Tomorrow, I got to wake up and depend on him. He's gonna depend on me.'
jokes.setup: Mac is going to bed
jokes.punchline: Mac has constructed an elaborate logical justification for going to sleep based entirely on his codependency with Dennis — presented as deep wisdom
jokes.explanation: Funny in its circular logic but slightly overstays its welcome. The core idea is strong — Mac has fully internalized codependency as a worldview — but the speech runs a beat long.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I could have been bashing your face in before you knew what hit you, which would've been this hammer, which I already had in my hand, in case you weren't listening.

jokes.text: Dee and Charlie stuck with each other: 'I kind of wanted to hang out with the guys, so...' 'I know. Me too. But they went to bed, so just you and me.' 'Yeah, but I-I don't want it to be.'
jokes.setup: Everyone else has gone to bed; Dee and Charlie are left alone
jokes.punchline: Both explicitly state they don't want to be with each other but are stuck — the blunt mutual disappointment played completely straight
jokes.explanation: The mutual disappointment is relatable and has a gentle comic truth to it — both characters know they're the B-tier of the group. Quiet but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: That old vegetable lady is your mom?

jokes.text: Frank has broken into the apartment of the man who saved him, is making him breakfast, and has already noted he grinds his teeth
jokes.setup: The man who performed the Heimlich on Frank is waking up normally
jokes.punchline: Frank has broken into his home, made himself at home, observed his teeth-grinding, and announced he's moving in — in the span of one night
jokes.explanation: Frank's total lack of social boundaries expressed as home invasion after one good deed is excellent. The detail about noticing he grinds his teeth — implying Frank watched him sleep — is a perfect understated horror detail.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I threw a sheet over her head. She was freaking me out.

jokes.text: Frank: 'You know how easy it was for me to get in that window? Took me all of 30 seconds with this hammer. I could have been bashing your face in before you knew what hit you, which would've been this hammer, which I already had in my hand, in case you weren't listening.'
jokes.setup: Frank is explaining how he broke into the man's home as a demonstration of security vulnerabilities
jokes.punchline: Frank clarifies that the thing that would have hit him was the hammer — which he already had in his hand — delivered as a helpful clarification rather than a threat
jokes.explanation: Frank explaining hammer-to-face physics as helpful clarification is very funny. The circular 'in case you weren't listening' coda — as if the man might have missed the hammer detail — perfectly captures Frank's bizarre social logic.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Are you insane?! We can't just play!

jokes.text: Frank: 'Oh. That old vegetable lady is your mom? Nah, you don't have to worry about her. I took care of her.' / 'I threw a sheet over her head. She was freaking me out.'
jokes.setup: The man reveals he lives with his mother; Frank says 'I took care of her' — implying something ominous
jokes.punchline: Frank's 'taking care of her' meant throwing a sheet over her head because she was 'freaking him out'
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection — 'I took care of her' played for maximum ominous effect before the mundane-but-insane reveal. 'She was freaking me out' as the reason is perfect Frank logic. The structure is clean and the punchline earns its reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Too hard. Too fast.

jokes.text: Frank: 'It's gonna take me a long time to bash through that door.'
jokes.setup: Man tells Frank to leave through the door; Frank had implied he'd use the window
jokes.punchline: Frank's concern is not that he was just threatening to break in through a door — it's that it would take a long time, implying he's genuinely calculating the effort
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Frank scene. The implication that Frank is genuinely calculating door-bashing time is both deeply unsettling and very funny. Economical and character-perfect exit line.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Pollen?! You didn't tell me there was to be pollen today.

jokes.text: Mac's pre-workout ritual for basketball: pre-workout shake, calf rub, ankle taping — before even starting to warm up
jokes.setup: Charlie wants to just play basketball
jokes.punchline: Dennis has an elaborate multi-step pre-workout routine that must be completed before any actual basketball occurs
jokes.explanation: Establishes the Mac-serves-Dennis dynamic in a new context. Competent but not exceptional — the joke is implicit in the description rather than landing in a specific line.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I went into the Puerto Rican part of town, started making fun of their big fat asses and asked them if they were Dominican.

jokes.text: Dennis's basketball warm-up plan: 15 minutes of passing, then light jog, then layups — and immediately throws the first pass too hard
jokes.setup: Dennis describes an extremely methodical warm-up plan
jokes.punchline: The very first pass is immediately too hard, then the second is also wrong — Dennis can't execute the most basic element of his own plan
jokes.explanation: Good visual comedy — Dennis's elaborate planning immediately destroyed by incompetent execution. The 'too hard. Too fast. Still a little bit too hard. Simple.' progression is a nice understated escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Take a break from your cockfighting and, uh, you know, hop in your rafts and come bring it to a real American

jokes.text: Dennis claims to feel unwell, then Mac announces there's pollen in the air — Dennis: 'Pollen?! You didn't tell me there was to be pollen today.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is already struggling at basketball when Mac mentions pollen
jokes.punchline: Dennis treats pollen as something Mac was responsible for disclosing in advance — as if weather conditions are Mac's duty to clear
jokes.explanation: Dennis treating pollen as Mac's administrative failure is a great character moment — his demands on Mac extend to controlling atmospheric conditions. 'You didn't tell me there was to be pollen today' is a quotable line.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That's Mexican!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That's Mexican.

jokes.text: Dee went into the Puerto Rican neighborhood and started making fun of their 'big fat asses' and asking if they were Dominican
jokes.setup: Dee explains her plan to get a rush from near-death experiences
jokes.punchline: Her method is racist provocation — she tried progressively more offensive things until she found one that worked, then led them back to the guys
jokes.explanation: Fully in Sunny's wheelhouse — the joke is on Dee for being a terrible person. The 'turns out they're a very lovely community, so I really had to dig deeper' detail is a good specific touch showing her escalating awfulness. Lands but doesn't transcend.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You would put us all at risk with your suicidal race-baiting.

jokes.text: I feel like the only way to truly live life to its fullest is to live it on the edge. / On the edge of what? / On the edge of life or death.
jokes.setup: Dee arrives to explain her new life philosophy, speaking with the gravity of someone who's had an epiphany.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's literal clarifying question — 'On the edge of what?' — deflates Dee's grandiosity; Dee's answer doubles down on the cliché, completely unaware that she's being mocked.
jokes.explanation: Charlie as accidental straight man is a consistent Sunny formula. His literal 'on the edge of what?' is a good deflating beat. Solid but familiar construction.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: I think she look nuts!

jokes.text: Dee: 'I was like, you guys, why don't you take a break from your cockfighting and hop in your rafts and come bring it to a real American?' [Charlie/Mac: 'That's Mexican!']
jokes.setup: Dee is describing the racial slurs she used to provoke the community
jokes.punchline: Even Charlie and Mac — not known for cultural sensitivity — immediately correct her that the stereotypes she's deploying are from the wrong group
jokes.explanation: The punchline is not the slurs themselves but that Charlie and Mac — the most ignorant characters on the show — immediately recognize she's using the wrong country's stereotypes. It's a layered joke about Dee's specific, compounded incompetence. 'That's Mexican!' from both of them in unison is a sharp choice.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: Made her dinner already. She's eating blue.

jokes.text: Dennis collapses claiming pollen depletion and 'Dee-shaming' have drained his electrolytes
jokes.setup: Dennis is suddenly very weak in the middle of the basketball court
jokes.punchline: Dennis invents 'Dee-shaming' as a legitimate energy-draining activity that has depleted his electrolytes alongside pollen exposure
jokes.explanation: 'Dee-shaming' as an official category of physical exertion that depletes electrolytes is a genuinely original Dennis-ism. The fact that he said it while (we now know) being secretly poisoned adds rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Somebody enrolled somebody back into pilot school.

jokes.text: Something's off. I-I got to go home. / You're leaving? / Yes. We were playing basketball, and I've depleted my electrolytes, and now I'm Dee-shaming, and that's depleted me even more.
jokes.setup: Dennis is suddenly, dramatically feeling unwell in the middle of the basketball court.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's explanation conflates his electrolyte levels with 'Dee-shaming' as equivalent energy drains — treating insulting his sister as a physical exertion that depletes him — which is both a great neologism and a perfect Dennis moment.
jokes.explanation: 'Dee-shaming' as a compound noun — casually coined as though it's a recognized activity that costs him energy — is an excellent Dennis coinage. The logic that insulting Dee is a physical exertion that depletes electrolytes is absurd in a very specific Dennis way. Highly quotable new Sunny vocabulary.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Blue has the most antioxygens.

jokes.text: Mac: 'He can count on me, guys.' — said to Charlie and Dee while helping Dennis walk home, repeated twice with increasing desperation
jokes.setup: Mac is helping Dennis home; Dennis is weakened
jokes.punchline: Mac keeps announcing to everyone that Dennis can count on him — the announcement undermining the act itself, performed for an audience rather than for Dennis
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Mac's acts of loyalty are always performative announcements rather than quiet deeds. Doesn't land as a huge joke but is thematically solid.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I want to throw this shake in your stupid face, but I'm struggling.

jokes.text: I'm wobbly. / Here. You can count on me, buddy. / All right, get me... / You can count on me. / Get me home. / He can count on me, guys.
jokes.setup: Dennis claims he's too weak to walk. Mac rushes to help him home.
jokes.punchline: Mac announces 'You can count on me' three times in escalating earnestness — first to Dennis, then as an aside to the group — revealing that this is entirely for Mac's own benefit, not Dennis's.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat on Mac's performative devotion. The triple repetition of 'you can count on me' escalates from sincere to self-serving in a classic Mac pattern. Reinforces the episode's themes without being particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dennis, do you want me to throw it into my own face?

jokes.text: Dee asks Charlie if he wants to take 'this beating' with her; long pause; Charlie: 'No.'
jokes.setup: An angry mob is presumably on its way; Dee asks Charlie to face it with her
jokes.punchline: Charlie's completely flat 'No.' after a pause — no elaboration, no apology
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the pause and single word says everything. Charlie's refusal to even engage with the proposition is the correct response and funnier for its brevity.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Are you feeding Dennis blended-up pizza and soda shakes?

jokes.text: Frank has broken into the man's home again, cooked his elderly mother a meal, and 'spruced her up' — she now looks insane
jokes.setup: Frank had been told to leave and not return
jokes.punchline: He's broken back in, cooked for the mother, and given her a makeover that makes her look 'nuts'
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Frank's intrusion — from breaking in once to full domestic takeover including a mother makeover — is funny. The visual of the 'spruced up' mother that makes her look 'nuts' is good dark comedy, though we can't see it.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I want him to depend on me to take care of him, to bring him back from the brink of death.

jokes.text: Frank has done homework on the man and re-enrolled him in pilot school without asking: 'Somebody enrolled somebody back into pilot school.'
jokes.setup: Frank has been digging through the man's private history
jokes.punchline: Frank presents the unauthorized re-enrollment in a school the man dropped out of — presented as a gift — with the passive 'somebody enrolled somebody' phrasing to distance himself from the invasion
jokes.explanation: 'Somebody enrolled somebody back into pilot school' is a brilliantly evasive construction. Frank both taking credit and disavowing the act simultaneously, using the passive voice as a shield, is very funny and character-specific. Frank's lack of boundaries masquerading as benevolence is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Munchausen by proxy, that's cute and everything. But if you want Dennis to really depend on you, you're gonna have to save his life... for real.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Blue has the most antioxygens.'
jokes.setup: Frank is feeding the mother blue food
jokes.punchline: 'Antioxygens' — a confident malapropism of 'antioxidants' delivered as scientific fact, also calling back the blue food fixation
jokes.explanation: 'Antioxygens' is a great malapropism — specific enough to be clearly wrong but close enough to show Frank tried. Combined with the episode-long blue food callback, this is a satisfying and quotable line. Frank's confident pseudoscience is a classic character note.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: She always said it's the last thing she ever wanted, so... So, thank you.

jokes.text: And not one of them bang 'em and bin 'em joints. Something really nice.
jokes.setup: Frank is offering to put the waiter's mother in a care home, stressing it will be quality.
jokes.punchline: Frank's phrase 'bang 'em and bin 'em joints' — a casual, filthy euphemism for low-quality nursing homes — reveals he is intimately familiar with the range of elder care options, from the horrifying to the merely bad.
jokes.explanation: 'Bang 'em and bin 'em joints' is an outstanding coinage — specific, filthy, and chilling. Only Frank Reynolds would know this term, use it casually, and think it's reassuring to bring up while promising a 'nice' home. The phrase itself is quotable far outside the episode's context. High originality because this specific piece of Frank-language is fresh.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm sticking her in a bang 'em and bin 'em joint.

jokes.text: Mac wants to throw Dennis's shake in his face but is 'struggling' — can't muster the strength to do it
jokes.setup: Mac is frustrated with Dennis; wants to throw the shake at him as an act of defiance
jokes.punchline: Mac is so weakened (or so neurologically conditioned by Dennis) that he literally cannot muster the energy to throw a drink
jokes.explanation: Good visual setup that leads into the three-way shake confusion scene. Mac's inability to perform even a defiant act against Dennis is thematically resonant.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: 15, 20 tops. Just until he flatlines. Then you bring him back.

jokes.text: The three-way shake confusion: Dennis wants Mac to throw it at Charlie; Mac wants to throw it at himself; Charlie offers to throw it at himself — all three are wrong about who should throw what at whom
jokes.setup: Dennis wants the shake thrown in Mac's face as a performative gesture
jokes.punchline: The gesture is completely destroyed by all three parties misunderstanding roles — Mac thinks Dennis wants it thrown at himself; Charlie offers his own face; Dennis: 'You've both ruined the moment.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedic construction. The escalating misunderstanding about who gets the shake thrown at them is very funny, and 'You've both ruined the moment' is a perfect Dennis exit line — he cares more about the theatrics than the outcome. The scene captures all three characters' specific pathologies simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Because it's poisoned!

jokes.text: Yeah. I'll carry you, because I... / No, no, no. You're not gonna... No. You dropped me twice last time. / You bumbling idiot.
jokes.setup: Mac offers to carry the weakened Dennis to bed.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's refusal reveals Mac has dropped him twice before — establishing this as an ongoing dynamic with a history — making 'bumbling idiot' an earned insult with specific precedent.
jokes.explanation: The 'dropped me twice last time' detail is great worldbuilding — there have been other times Mac has carried Dennis, and failed. Treats the audience like they should know this history even if they don't. Earned through character logic.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I don't need you to tell me what to do, Dennis. I'm going to make my own decision.

jokes.text: Charlie tastes the shake and notes it tastes like pizza and soda; Mac claims it's 'pizza-flavored' protein shake
jokes.setup: Charlie wants to drink Dennis's shake
jokes.punchline: The shake actually tastes like pizza and soda because it IS blended pizza and soda — Mac's fumbling lie ('that's probably just the pizza-flavored one') is immediately transparent
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — the audience and Charlie simultaneously discover the shake is literal blended pizza. Mac's pathetic cover story ('pizza-flavored one') is correctly transparent. Sets up the Munchausen revelation nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I saw it! I saw the other side. I didn't like it. I hated it. It was just blackness.

jokes.text: Are you feeding Dennis blended-up pizza and soda shakes? / Shh. Yes. Uh, I'm poisoning him, all right? Just... A little bit.
jokes.setup: Charlie has figured out the shake is pizza and soda blended together.
jokes.punchline: Mac's response — 'I'm poisoning him, all right? Just... A little bit.' — is delivered with the guilty defensiveness of someone caught in a minor misdeed, not attempted murder. 'A little bit' is the key qualifier.
jokes.explanation: 'I'm poisoning him, all right? Just... A little bit.' is an exceptional confession. The 'a little bit' qualifier treats poisoning as a matter of degree, as though a small amount of intentional poisoning is a reasonable and defensible position. Mac's tone — embarrassed but not apologetic — is the perfect delivery for this reveal. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Mac's confession: he's been slowly poisoning Dennis with blended pizza and soda to make him weak and dependent — 'Munchausen by proxy'
jokes.setup: Charlie has figured out the shake is blended pizza
jokes.punchline: Mac admits he's been poisoning Dennis to make him physically dependent on Mac's care — described by Dee as 'Munchausen by proxy'
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Mac's care for Dennis is actually a slow poisoning scheme is an excellent Sunny dark-comedy twist. It retroactively recontextualizes everything Mac has done in the episode (the shake obsession, the calf rub, the ankle tape). The Munchausen by proxy diagnosis is accurate and funny. This is one of the episode's best reveals.

jokes.text: Dee free-soloed the building to deliver her counter-plan: 'Sucked though. Didn't feel a thing.'
jokes.setup: Dee arrives through what appears to be a window after scaling the building
jokes.punchline: Dee free-soloed a building for a thrill but felt nothing — her thrill-seeking is becoming increasingly dangerous and decreasingly satisfying
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of Dee's arc — she's progressed from 'nearly hit by Uber' to 'free-soloed a building' in one day, with diminishing returns. The flat 'Didn't feel a thing' is a solid deadpan button.

jokes.text: Dee: 'Mac, Munchausen by proxy, that's cute and everything. But if you want Dennis to really depend on you, you're gonna have to save his life... for real.'
jokes.setup: Mac has been slowly poisoning Dennis; Dee proposes a better plan
jokes.punchline: Dee proposes actually engineering a near-death situation to save Dennis from — genuinely topping Mac's already dark scheme
jokes.explanation: Dee's casual dismissal of Munchausen by proxy as 'cute' and her counter-proposal of an actual staged near-death experience is a good escalation. Character-specific: Dee's thrill-seeking now redirected into schemes.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Well, three of the things are still in plastic packaging.'
jokes.setup: Frank has prepared a 'blue feast' but the man hesitates to eat it
jokes.punchline: Frank's feast — presumably elaborate-looking — includes items still in their original plastic packaging, which Frank delivers as an observation rather than a problem
jokes.explanation: Frank's total unawareness that unpacking food is a step in meal preparation is funny. The deadpan delivery ('well, three of the things') implies this is a known fact he's sharing, not a problem he's aware of.

jokes.text: The man reveals his mother explicitly said being put in a home was 'the last thing she ever wanted' — Frank put her in one anyway
jokes.setup: Frank presented putting the mother in a home as a generous act
jokes.punchline: The mother had repeatedly said that was the worst possible fate; Frank ignored this entirely
jokes.explanation: Good reversal of Frank's generosity — his gift was actually the thing the person most feared. Frank's obliviousness to others' stated wishes is consistent character comedy.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Well, I told you not to because I was sticking her in a bang 'em and bin 'em joint. They're much cheaper!'
jokes.setup: Frank had told the man not to visit his mother to 'avoid the emotion of it all'
jokes.punchline: Frank's real reason: he put her in a cheap, disreputable facility — a 'bang 'em and bin 'em joint' — after promising a nice one
jokes.explanation: 'Bang 'em and bin 'em joint' is an exceptional coinage — vivid, horrible, and totally Frank Reynolds. The reveal that Frank's generous facade concealed a cheap elder-care scam is perfectly dark. The phrase is quotable, shocking, and deeply character-specific. One of the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: If you think I'm paying the 40 grand you owe that flight school, you got another thing coming! / I owe them? I can't afford that. / Yes! / Well, then you probably can't afford the bin 'em joint, 'cause that shit ain't free, bozo!
jokes.setup: Frank and the waiter's relationship is rapidly unraveling.
jokes.punchline: Frank's escalating financial accusations — enrolling the waiter in pilot school he now owes 40k for, while also having put his mother in a home he now has to pay for — culminate in Frank calling him 'bozo,' an oddly vintage insult.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation on Frank's pattern of doing 'favors' that create financial obligations. The reveal that enrolling someone in pilot school creates a 40k debt — and Frank immediately weaponizing this — is a classic Frank hustle. 'Bozo' as the parting insult from a man who just described elder abuse facilities is a tonal choice.

jokes.text: Dee's plan: powder that seizes Dennis's throat, wait 15-20 minutes until he flatlines, then use EpiPen
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are planning to stage a near-death experience for Dennis
jokes.punchline: Dee's plan involves actually letting Dennis flatline for up to 20 minutes before intervening — presented as a reasonable timeline
jokes.explanation: '15, 20 tops. Just until he flatlines. Then you bring him back.' Dee's casual calibration of near-death timing is very funny. The 'tops' qualifier, as if she's being generous with the flatline window, is the right comedic word.

jokes.text: Mac's counter-argument for not poisoning Dennis: 'You don't think Dennis is gonna see right through this silly ruse?' — he objects to the intelligence failure, not the ethics
jokes.setup: Dee proposes poisoning Dennis; Mac objects
jokes.punchline: Mac's objection is not 'we shouldn't poison Dennis' but 'Dennis is too smart, he'll see through it' — the ethics are not a factor
jokes.explanation: Mac's moral framework — he's not against poisoning, just against plans that won't work — is perfectly in character. The objection being tactical rather than ethical is a sharp piece of character comedy.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'So that's why we invited Frank. Because Charlie and I can jump to action and save Frank's life. Together.'
jokes.setup: Mac is explaining the scheme's logic
jokes.punchline: The plan is to poison Frank — an innocent bystander — to stage a rescue for Dennis's benefit
jokes.explanation: The casual decision to use Frank as an unwitting prop in their scheme — after Frank already choked once this episode — is a good dark callback to the episode's premise.

jokes.text: Dee: 'Listen, consider the flatline though, okay? 'Cause I really got to know what people see on the other side.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are discussing their scheme
jokes.punchline: Dee's personal motivation for the plan is scientific curiosity about the afterlife — she wants to use this as an opportunity to research near-death experiences
jokes.explanation: Good character note — Dee's thrill-seeking has evolved into genuine metaphysical curiosity, and she's willing to briefly kill someone to satisfy it. Sets up her actual near-death experience at the episode's end.

jokes.text: The hated waiter appears at the restaurant again begging for his job back: 'I'm just here to beg for my job back, thanks to this guy.'
jokes.setup: Second restaurant scene; the gang has presumably gotten the waiter fired
jokes.punchline: The waiter's third appearance — now having lost his job — the gang's inescapable wake of destruction follows him
jokes.explanation: The running gag of the inescapable waiter now deepened by the gang having destroyed his career. 'Do I know you?' from Dennis/Frank is the right oblivious response.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Do I know you?' — responding to the waiter who served him through a near-fatal choking episode
jokes.setup: The waiter says the gang got him fired
jokes.punchline: Frank has no memory of the waiter who was present during his choking — a character who has appeared multiple times is unrecognized
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the waiter running gag. Frank's complete non-recognition after a traumatic shared experience is consistent with the gang's total self-centeredness.

jokes.text: Charlie's sharpened teeth reveal: 'I sharpened my teeth, FYI.'
jokes.setup: The gang is making peace offerings at the restaurant
jokes.punchline: Charlie has actually sharpened his teeth — taking Frank's earlier complaint seriously — delivered as a minor logistical update
jokes.explanation: Exceptional callback execution. The fact that Charlie actually went and had his teeth sharpened — taking this absurd detail seriously as a point of pride — is funny and deeply character-specific. 'FYI' as the delivery mechanism is perfect economy. The callback to the opening scene pays off with full Charlie commitment.

jokes.text: The shake confusion scene: Frank wants it, Dennis wants it, Mac forbids it, everyone arguing about who gets the poisoned shake
jokes.setup: Mac has brought a poisoned shake to the restaurant for Frank
jokes.punchline: Everyone wants to drink the poisoned shake — Dennis because he thinks the shakes have been helping him; Frank out of random desire — and Mac keeps trying to redirect it correctly
jokes.explanation: The irony of Dennis actively wanting the shake that's been making him sick — because he thinks it's been helping — is excellent dark comedy. The chaos of everyone wanting the poison is a good escalation of the scheme's premise.

jokes.text: Mac blurts out 'Because it's poisoned!' to prevent Dennis from drinking the shake
jokes.setup: Frank insists Dennis should have the shake; Mac is running out of options
jokes.punchline: Mac reveals the poison to save Dennis — the scheme collapsing because Mac cannot allow Dennis to be harmed, even by Mac's own poison
jokes.explanation: The reveal lands well — Mac's compulsive protection of Dennis overrides even his own scheme. 'Because it's poisoned!' as a helpless blurt is very funny, and the stunned reactions ('Excuse me?', 'It has a little bit of poison in it.') as everyone normalizes it are perfect.

jokes.text: Gang casually confirms multiple times the shake is poisoned: 'It has a little bit of poison in it.' 'It has poison in it.' 'It's got... It's poisoned.' 'It's poisoned.'
jokes.setup: Mac has revealed the shake is poisoned
jokes.punchline: Everyone in turn confirms the poison with slightly different phrasing — the chorus of 'yes, the poison thing' treated as mundane news
jokes.explanation: The repeated low-key confirmations of poison by multiple characters — each slightly redundant — creates a funny rhythm. The gang treating 'yes, it's poisoned' as minor news is very Sunny. The structure of the escalating repetition with diminishing variation is well-calibrated.

jokes.text: Frank: 'You were gonna poison me, Charlie?' / Charlie: 'Yeah.' / 'And I was as well.'
jokes.setup: Frank has just learned the shake was poisoned for him
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately confirms yes, and Mac chimes in that he also was going to poison Frank — said with a slightly competitive air
jokes.explanation: Charlie's flat 'Yeah.' to 'you were going to poison me?' is perfect, but Mac's addition of 'And I was as well' — with its slightly formal phrasing suggesting he wants credit — is the funnier beat. Mac's need to be included in the poisoning is exactly right.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie: 'But I was gonna save you, dude.' / 'Me, too.' / 'Like, right afterward.' / 'Immediately.'
jokes.setup: Frank is upset about being targeted for poisoning
jokes.punchline: Both Mac and Charlie fall over each other to emphasize how quickly they would have saved him — 'right afterward' / 'immediately' — competitive in their reassurance
jokes.explanation: The competitive reassurance escalation — 'right afterward' one-upped by 'immediately' — is a good comedic rhythm. Each character trying to establish they were the more prompt would-be rescuer.

jokes.text: Mac glomming on to Charlie's plan to also save Frank: 'And I had your back, too, with the plan. I was gonna... do the plan... and save Frank.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has apologized to Frank and said he'll always save him
jokes.punchline: Mac tries to claim equal credit for the plan he joined late, with the barely-articulated 'do the plan' as his contribution
jokes.explanation: Mac's pathetic attempt to claim credit for a plan he co-opted is consistent but not exceptional. 'Do the plan' as a vague description is a mild laugh.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'So you were still gonna rely on a decision that somebody else made, only, this time, you were potentially gonna kill a man?'
jokes.setup: Mac explains he was going to follow Charlie's plan to save Frank
jokes.punchline: Dennis identifies the problem: Mac outsourced the decision-making again, just this time in a plan involving homicide
jokes.explanation: Dennis's precise articulation of Mac's character flaw — applied to a poisoning scheme — is an excellent episode callback and character moment. The structure is tight: the same pathology (outsourcing decisions) escalated to manslaughter-level stakes.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Are you not pleased?'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just pointed out that Mac's plan involved potentially killing someone
jokes.punchline: Mac's response is genuine inquiry about whether Dennis is pleased with the effort — the murder-adjacent scheme evaluated purely on whether it impressed Dennis
jokes.explanation: The best line in the episode. Four words that perfectly encapsulate Mac's entire character arc, his relationship with Dennis, and the show's dark comedy thesis. After all the scheming, the poisoning, the manipulation — Mac's only frame of reference is 'did this please Dennis?' The formal register ('Are you not pleased?' rather than 'Are you happy?') makes it even funnier. This is quotable, character-defining, and structurally perfect. It's not quite the Snip Snap anchor, but it's in that tier for this episode.

jokes.text: Dee has accidentally drunk the poisoned shake and is unresponsive on the floor
jokes.setup: Everyone has been arguing about who gets the shake; Dee apparently got it
jokes.punchline: Dee is on the floor having drunk the poison she helped design — the ironic victim of her own scheme
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural payoff — Dee designed the scheme to explore near-death experiences and ends up accidentally being its victim. The irony is clean and well-earned. The chaos of the shake fight makes it believable that Dee got it.

jokes.text: Mac refuses to use the EpiPen on Dee without Dennis's permission: 'I don't need you to tell me what to do, Dennis. I'm going to make my own decision.'
jokes.setup: Dee is dying; Dennis tells Mac to use the EpiPen
jokes.punchline: Mac, in his desperate attempt to demonstrate independence, refuses to use the EpiPen when told to — letting Dee come closer to death as a point of principle about autonomous decision-making
jokes.explanation: This is the structural and thematic climax of the episode — the perfect payoff for the entire Mac-Dennis dependency arc. Mac's decision to prove his independence by NOT using the EpiPen while Dee dies is both hilarious and a savage indictment of his character. The irony is devastating: in finally making his own decision, he makes the worst possible one. The callback architecture is impeccable. This rivals 'Are you not pleased?' as the episode's best joke.

jokes.text: That's okay. I have this. / Uh, okay. / Hit her with it, man. / All right, go. / No. / I'm telling you to do it. / I don't need you to tell me what to do, Dennis. I'm going to make my own decision.
jokes.setup: Mac has the EpiPen. Dee is dying. Dennis tells Mac to use it.
jokes.punchline: Mac refuses to use the EpiPen specifically BECAUSE Dennis told him to — choosing this moment, with Dee's life on the line, to assert independence from Dennis's direction. The worst possible moment for a character stand.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional callback and character payoff. The entire episode has been about Mac's inability to act without Dennis's instruction. Here, with Dee actively dying, Mac finally chooses THIS moment to assert independence — specifically BECAUSE Dennis told him what to do. The irony is devastating and perfectly constructed. This is the thematic and comedic climax of the entire episode's A-plot. Comparable to an 8.5+ anchor joke in terms of construction and character specificity.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'She wanted to see the other side, and I want Dennis to see that I can make my own decision.'
jokes.setup: Dee is dying; Mac is refusing to administer the EpiPen
jokes.punchline: Mac explains his dual motivation: Dee wanted this (near-death research), and Mac wants Dennis to witness his autonomous decision-making — letting someone die as an act of self-expression
jokes.explanation: Mac's rationalization — 'this is what Dee wanted AND it proves my independence to Dennis' — perfectly merges both characters' arcs into one moment. The fact that this logic is offered while Dee is unresponsive on the floor is excellent dark comedy.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Oh, my God! What is wrong with you people?!'
jokes.setup: Mac is refusing to administer the EpiPen on principle; Dee is dying
jokes.punchline: Frank — who earlier this episode was left to choke to death by these same people — is now the voice of moral outrage
jokes.explanation: Perfect ironic callback — Frank, the episode's original choking victim, is now outraged that someone isn't being saved from choking. He's achieved no self-awareness but is correctly horrified. The structural irony is elegant and doesn't need explanation.

jokes.text: Dee's near-death report: 'I saw it! I saw the other side. I didn't like it. I hated it. It was just blackness. There's nothing there. It's just dark. That's it. Just lights out. I don't want to do that anymore.'
jokes.setup: Dee has been revived from an anaphylactic episode
jokes.punchline: Dee's afterlife report — which she risked her life to obtain — is devastatingly anticlimactic: just darkness, nothing, 'lights out'
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff to Dee's arc. She risked everyone's lives (and her own) to discover the afterlife, and it's just nothing. The escalating disappointment in her description ('I didn't like it. I hated it.') is well-structured. The existential nihilism is very Sunny — the universe has no rewards for bad people.

jokes.text: Charlie/Frank: 'Hey, dude, can we get some, like, bread sticks and menus and, you know...' / 'Dinner and a show.'
jokes.setup: Dee has just been revived from near-death; chaos is subsiding
jokes.punchline: The immediate pivot to ordering food — plus 'dinner and a show' as an assessment of the evening — treats the near-death experience as an entertainment amenity
jokes.explanation: 'Dinner and a show' as the final line — with a near-death experience as the 'show' — is a good economical button for the episode. Treats Dee's trauma as a minor inconvenience and an entertainment bonus.

tmdb_overview: Annoyed that the Gang failed to react as he nearly choked to death on an appetizer, Frank decides the Waiter, his savior, is the only person who has his back.
